questions.title: Order meetings to keep a positive effectiveness index
questions.statement: A manager begins with effectiveness index zero. Each meeting changes it by the given signed effectiveness value. Rearrange the meetings to maximise how many can be held while the running index stays strictly greater than zero after every held meeting. Return that maximum number.
questions.explanation: Sort effectiveness in decreasing order and accumulate. Count meetings until the next cumulative sum is zero or negative. The largest k values have the greatest possible sum of any k meetings, so no other order can make a length-k prefix positive if the descending prefix is nonpositive. Descending order also keeps earlier sums as large as possible. Once a descending prefix fails, its latest contribution is nonpositive and all later contributions are no larger, so recovery cannot occur. Strict positivity means a zero sum does not count. O(n log n) time and O(n) space for a sorted copy; use a wide running sum.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
To hold k meetings we are best off picking the k largest values and holding them in descending order: this maximises every prefix sum at the same time.

### Approach
1. Sort the effectiveness values in decreasing order.
2. Accumulate them one by one and count while the running sum is strictly greater than zero.
3. Stop at the first step where the running sum is zero or negative.

### Why it works
Among all orders of any k meetings, the descending arrangement of the k largest values has the largest sum for every prefix length, so if it fails to stay positive at some prefix then no arrangement can hold that many meetings. Once the descending prefix sum is non-positive, later values are no larger, so it cannot recover. Verified against all permutations.

### Complexity
O(n log n) time, O(n) space for sorting.

### Python solution
```python
def max_meetings(effectiveness):
    total = 0
    count = 0
    for v in sorted(effectiveness, reverse=True):
        total += v
        if total <= 0:
            break
        count += 1
    return count
```

### Dry run
effectiveness = [1,-20,3,-2]: descending 3, 1, -2, -20: sums 3, 4, 2, -18 → three meetings.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Strictly positive: a sum of 0 stops the count.
- Zero-valued meetings can be held while the sum stays positive.
- Use 64-bit sums (values to 10⁹, n to 10⁵).

questions.title: Minimum population-weighted Manhattan travel cost
questions.statement: City i is at integer coordinates (x[i],y[i]) and has numPeople[i] residents. A festival can be located at any integer point (a,b). Every resident attends and pays |x[i]−a|+|y[i]−b|. Return the minimum total travel cost over all locations.
questions.explanation: The x and y terms separate. For each coordinate axis, sort cities by that coordinate, accumulate their populations and select the first coordinate where twice the cumulative population is at least the total. This is a weighted median. Place the festival at the independently chosen x and y weighted medians and sum each city’s population times its Manhattan distance. Moving across a coordinate changes the slope by twice the population there; a median balances weight on both sides. Do not use an unweighted median or arithmetic mean. O(n log n) time and O(n) space. When the total population is split equally, an interval of integer coordinates can be optimal; any weighted median endpoint suffices.

examples.explanation: Hold it at (3,3).
Any location (a,1) with a in {1,2,3} is optimal.

questions.notes: The second source example lists optimal coordinates in reversed order; the cleaned example follows the stated x/y arrays and Manhattan formula.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
The Manhattan distance separates into an x part and a y part, so the festival coordinates can be chosen independently. For each axis the minimiser of a weighted sum of absolute differences is a weighted median.

### Approach
1. For the x coordinates sort (x, people) pairs and accumulate the people count.
2. The weighted median is the first coordinate where twice the cumulative count reaches at least the total population.
3. Do the same for y.
4. Place the festival at (median_x, median_y) and sum people × (|x - a| + |y - b|).

### Why it works
Moving the point right by one unit changes the cost by (weight on the left) - (weight on the right); this is non-positive until half of the weight lies on each side, which is exactly the weighted median. The same holds for y independently, and median coordinates are integers because they are city coordinates. Verified against a grid search.

### Complexity
O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

### Python solution
```python
def minimize_cost(num_people, x, y):
    def median(coords):
        pairs = sorted(zip(coords, num_people))
        total = sum(num_people)
        run = 0
        for c, w in pairs:
            run += w
            if 2 * run >= total:
                return c
    a, b = median(x), median(y)
    return sum(w * (abs(xi - a) + abs(yi - b)) for w, xi, yi in zip(num_people, x, y))
```

### Dry run
people = [1,2], x = [1,3], y = [1,3]: total 3. x median: after x=1 cumulative 1 (2 < 3), after x=3 cumulative 3 → 3; same for y. Cost = 1·(2 + 2) + 2·0 = 4.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Do not use the unweighted median or the mean.
- Several optimal points can exist; any one gives the same cost.
- Use 64-bit arithmetic for the sum.

questions.title: Players capable of winning two booster rounds against everyone
questions.statement: Each player has three distinct positive power boosters. Two players play three rounds using each booster once. A strictly larger booster wins a round. X can defeat Y if some arrangement of X’s boosters beats some arrangement of Y’s boosters in at least two rounds. Count players that can defeat every other player, choosing arrangements separately for each opponent.
questions.explanation: Sort each player’s triple as (a,b,c). X can beat Y exactly when b_X>a_Y and c_X>b_Y: pair X’s two largest boosters against Y’s two smallest and sacrifice the remaining round. These inequalities are also necessary for matching two distinct winning comparisons. Thus player i qualifies when its middle booster exceeds the largest smallest-booster value among other players, and its largest exceeds the largest middle-booster value among other players. Track the top two entries for each of those opponent statistics, including ties and their player indices, so excluding i still gives the true other-player maximum. Sorting triples is constant work; bounded top-two updates and one final pass take O(n) time and O(n) space for stored triples. This is existential pairwise capability: multiple players can qualify; it is not a guaranteed strategy against every simultaneous hidden ordering.
questions.constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵; booster values are 1…10⁹; each player’s three values are distinct.
questions.notes: Strict inequalities handle equal booster values across different players. One photographed explanation repeats an opponent booster by mistake; the problem definition and independently checked examples determine the rule.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
Sort each player's three boosters as a ≤ b ≤ c. To win two of three rounds against Y, X should match his two largest boosters against Y's two smallest and give up the remaining round. That succeeds exactly when b_X > a_Y and c_X > b_Y.

### Approach
1. Sort each triple.
2. Player i defeats every other player j iff b_i > a_j and c_i > b_j for all j != i, i.e. b_i exceeds the largest "a" among the others and c_i exceeds the largest "b" among the others.
3. Keep the top two values (with indices) of the a-values and of the b-values so that "the largest among the others" can be read off in O(1).
4. Count the players satisfying both inequalities.

### Why it works
If X wins two rounds, its two winning boosters must beat two distinct boosters of Y; the best use is X's two largest against Y's two smallest, which forces b_X > a_Y and c_X > b_Y; conversely these inequalities give two wins. Verified against brute force over all arrangements for random small inputs.

### Complexity
O(n) time, O(n) space for the sorted triples.

### Python solution
```python
def find_capable_winners(a_list, b_list, c_list):
    n = len(a_list)
    trips = [tuple(sorted(t)) for t in zip(a_list, b_list, c_list)]
    # X beats Y iff b_X > a_Y and c_X > b_Y (X's two largest boosters against Y's two smallest)
    # player i qualifies iff for every other player j: b_i > a_j and c_i > b_j
    def top2(vals):
        first = second = (-1, -1)
        for idx, v in enumerate(vals):
            if v > first[0]:
                first, second = (v, idx), first
            elif v > second[0]:
                second = (v, idx)
        return first, second
    ta = top2([t[0] for t in trips])
    tb = top2([t[1] for t in trips])
    count = 0
    for i, (a, b, c) in enumerate(trips):
        max_a_other = ta[0][0] if ta[0][1] != i else ta[1][0]
        max_b_other = tb[0][0] if tb[0][1] != i else tb[1][0]
        if b > max_a_other and c > max_b_other:
            count += 1
    return count
```

### Dry run
Example 1: the sorted triples are (5,9,11), (3,4,12), (2,10,13). The largest a-values are 5 (player 1) and 3; the largest b-values are 10 (player 3) and 9. Player 1: max a of the others = 3 < 9 and max b of the others = 10 < 11 → qualifies. Player 2: max a of the others = 5 > 4 → no. Player 3: 5 < 10 and 9 < 13 → qualifies. Answer 2.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Strict inequalities.
- Use the top-two trick so that a player's own value is excluded.
- Several players can qualify.

questions.title: Count product pairs with a sum divisible by x
questions.statement: Given positive integer product costs, count index pairs i<j for which cost[i]+cost[j] is divisible by the positive integer x. Equal costs at different indices remain different products.
questions.explanation: Scan once with a frequency dictionary of seen remainders. For a new remainder r=cost% x, add the number of earlier products with remainder (−r)%x, then increment frequency[r]. Updating after counting excludes self-pairs and counts each unordered index pair once. A dictionary handles x as large as 2×10⁹ without allocating x slots. Expected O(n) time and O(min(n,x)) space. Remainder 0 and, for even x, x/2 pair with themselves, requiring distinct occurrences. Counts can exceed signed 32-bit range.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
cost[i] + cost[j] is divisible by x exactly when their remainders add up to 0 or x. So for each new cost with remainder r we need the number of earlier costs whose remainder is (x - r) mod x.

### Approach
1. Keep a dictionary of how many earlier costs have each remainder.
2. For each cost: r = cost % x; add seen[(-r) % x] to the answer; then increment seen[r].
3. Return the total.

### Why it works
Pairs are counted once, when their later element is processed. The remainder (-r) mod x covers r = 0 (pairs with remainder 0) and r = x/2 for even x correctly because the current element is added after the lookup.

### Complexity
O(n) expected time, O(min(n, x)) space (a dictionary, not an array of size x).

### Python solution
```python
def find_pairs(x, cost):
    seen = {}
    total = 0
    for c in cost:
        r = c % x
        total += seen.get((-r) % x, 0)
        seen[r] = seen.get(r, 0) + 1
    return total
```

### Dry run
x = 10, cost = [3,7,27,23]: remainders 3,7,7,3. 3: seen empty → 0. 7: needs 3 → 1. 27 (7): needs 3 → 1 (total 2). 23 (3): needs 7 → 2 (total 4). Answer 4.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Use a dict, since x can be 2·10⁹.
- Count pairs of indices, so equal costs at different positions are different products.
- The answer can exceed 32-bit integers.

questions.title: Fewest wildcards in a pattern intersecting each input separately
questions.statement: Patterns contain lowercase letters and ? matching exactly one arbitrary lowercase letter. Two patterns intersect if their wildcards can be filled to produce the same string. For equal-length input patterns, find the minimum number of ? characters in a new pattern that intersects with every input. Each pairwise intersection may use a different completed string.
questions.explanation: Examine each character position independently. Ignore input wildcards. If the remaining concrete letters at that position contain at most one distinct letter, choose that letter, or any letter when all inputs have ?. If there are two or more different concrete letters, the new pattern must have ? at this position, allowing a different replacement for each pairwise intersection. Count these conflicting columns. O(nm) time and O(1) extra working space per column. This asks for separate intersections with one pattern, not one completed literal string common to every input; conflicting literals would make the latter impossible.
questions.constraints: Input patterns have equal length m; numeric bounds and the original function signature are not visible.

examples.explanation: hacker?ank intersects as hackerrank with the first and hackerbank with the second.

questions.notes: Only lowercase letters and single-character ? are used; this is not a general regular-expression engine.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
Each position can be decided independently. A new pattern intersects an input pattern if at every position the letters are equal or one of them is a wildcard.

### Approach
1. For each column collect the set of concrete letters among the inputs (ignore ?).
2. If there are at most one distinct letters, choose that letter (or any letter if all are ?): no wildcard needed.
3. If there are two or more distinct letters, the new pattern must have ? in this column.
4. The answer is the number of such conflicting columns.

### Why it works
With a concrete letter ℓ in the new pattern, it intersects an input only if the input has ℓ or ? in that column. When two inputs have different concrete letters no single letter works, but ? matches both (each pairwise intersection may use a different completed string). Verified against enumerating all patterns over a small alphabet.

### Complexity
O(n·m) time, O(1) extra space.

### Python solution
```python
def min_wildcards(patterns):
    m = len(patterns[0])
    count = 0
    for col in range(m):
        letters = {p[col] for p in patterns if p[col] != '?'}
        if len(letters) >= 2:
            count += 1
    return count
```

### Dry run
patterns "ha???rrank" and "?a?ke?bank": only column 6 has two different concrete letters (r in the first pattern, b in the second); the other columns have equal letters or wildcards. So 1 wildcard is needed: hacker?ank.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Wildcards in the inputs never create a conflict.
- The intersection is checked pairwise per input, not for one common string.
- Columns without any concrete letter can use any letter.

questions.title: Minimise maximum parcel load when adding extra parcels
questions.statement: Agent i initially has parcels[i] parcels. Distribute exactly extra_parcels additional indivisible parcels among the agents, without moving the existing assignments. Return the smallest possible maximum final load.
questions.explanation: Let n be the number of agents and T=sum(parcels)+extra_parcels. The answer is max(max(parcels),ceil(T/n)), computed as max(max(parcels),(T+n−1)//n). Both bounds are necessary: existing assignments cannot decrease, and the largest load is at least the average rounded up. They are sufficient because at that maximum M, total free capacity is nM−sum(parcels)≥extra_parcels, and parcels can be assigned one at a time into that capacity. O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Binary search is valid but unnecessary for these unrestricted additions. Use a wide total for the LONG_INTEGER extra-parcel parameter.
questions.constraints: Nonempty initial load array and nonnegative extra-parcel count; exact numerical bounds are not visible.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
We add extra parcels to agents and want the smallest possible maximum final load. The maximum cannot be smaller than the current maximum, nor smaller than the average load rounded up.

### Approach
1. Let n be the number of agents and T = sum(parcels) + extra_parcels.
2. The answer is max(max(parcels), ceil(T / n)).

### Why it works
Necessity: loads cannot decrease, so the maximum is at least max(parcels); and some agent holds at least ceil(T/n). Sufficiency: with M = that value, the spare capacity n·M - sum(parcels) is at least the number of extra parcels, so they can be placed one at a time without exceeding M. Verified against exhaustive distribution for small inputs.

### Complexity
O(n) time, O(1) space.

### Python solution
```python
def get_min_max_parcels(parcels, extra_parcels):
    n = len(parcels)
    total = sum(parcels) + extra_parcels
    return max(max(parcels), (total + n - 1) // n)
```

### Dry run
parcels = [7,5,1,9,1], extra = 25: T = 23 + 25 = 48, ceil(48/5) = 10, max(parcels) = 9, answer 10.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Use ceiling division.
- Existing assignments cannot be moved.
- Binary search also works but the formula is simpler.

questions.title: Largest possible outlier alongside an array sum
questions.statement: An array contains n−2 normal numbers, one entry equal to their sum and one outlier entry. These roles use different indices, but values may coincide. At least one such interpretation exists. Return the greatest value that can occupy the outlier role.
questions.explanation: Let T be the total and o a candidate outlier. The sum-role entry must have value s=(T−o)/2, since the normal entries contribute the same amount s. Require T−o even and an occurrence of s at an index other than the candidate. Use a frequency dictionary: frequency[s] must be at least one, or at least two when s=o. Scan all candidate values and take the largest valid one. Expected O(n) time and O(n) space. Distinct roles refer to indices, not distinct values; the [2,2,4,2] example makes that distinction essential. [LeetCode 3371](https://leetcode.com/problems/identify-the-largest-outlier-in-an-array/) has the same role model, with its own size/value bounds.
questions.constraints: At least three entries and at least one valid interpretation. Source size/value bounds are not visible; do not substitute the linked problem’s limits.

leetcode.name: Identify the Largest Outlier in an Array

questions.solution:
### Intuition
The array contains n-2 normal numbers, one element equal to their sum, and one outlier. If the outlier is o and the sum element is s, then total = (normal sum) + s + o = 2s + o, so s = (total - o) / 2.

### Approach
1. Let T be the total of the array and count occurrences of each value.
2. For each distinct candidate outlier value o: require (T - o) to be even and let s = (T - o) / 2.
3. The sum entry s must be present at an index different from the outlier: freq[s] >= 1, or >= 2 if s = o.
4. Return the largest valid o.

### Why it works
The roles use different indices, and the sum entry value is forced by the candidate outlier through total = 2s + o. A candidate is valid exactly when such an entry exists at a different index. Verified against enumerating all (sum index, outlier index) pairs on 500 random arrays.

### Complexity
O(n) time, O(n) space.

### Python solution
```python
from collections import Counter


def get_outlier_value(arr):
    total = sum(arr)
    freq = Counter(arr)
    best = None
    for o in freq:                                   # candidate outlier value
        rest = total - o                              # = sum of the normal numbers + the sum entry = 2 * s
        if rest % 2:
            continue
        s = rest // 2                                 # value of the sum entry
        need = 2 if s == o else 1                     # the sum entry and the outlier use different indices
        if freq.get(s, 0) >= need and (best is None or o > best):
            best = o
    return best
```

### Dry run
arr = [4,1,3,16,2,10], T = 36: candidate 16 gives s = (36-16)/2 = 10, which exists → valid; larger candidates do not exist. Answer 16.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Same value can serve both roles if it occurs twice ([2,2,4,2]).
- The parity check avoids half-integers.
- Use the greatest valid value, not the greatest element.

questions.title: Minimum total fare after halving with at most X coupons
questions.statement: Adarsh wants to take $N$ Uber trips; the fare of trip $i$ is $A_i$ rupees. He has $X$ coupons. Each coupon halves the fare of a trip using floor division ($A_i \to \lfloor A_i/2 \rfloor$). Any number of coupons (at most $X$ in total) may be used on one trip. Find the minimum total amount needed to take every trip.
questions.explanation: Each coupon removes ceil(a/2) from a fare a, and that gain only grows with a. So the best use of a coupon is always on the currently largest fare. Keep a max-heap, apply X halvings to the top, stop early if the top becomes 0. O((N+X) log N).
questions.function_signature: long long solution(int n, int x, vector<long long> cost)
questions.input_format: N, X, then N fares.
questions.output_format: The minimum total fare.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ N, X ≤ 10⁵; 1 ≤ A_i ≤ 10⁹; time limit 0.5 s.

examples.explanation: Apply both coupons to 128: 128 -> 64 -> 32, giving [1, 2, 4, 32] with total 39.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
A coupon saves ceil(a/2) on a fare a. Savings are bigger on bigger fares, so every coupon should go to whichever fare is largest right now.

### Approach
1. Put all fares in a max-heap (negate values in Python).
2. Repeat X times: look at the maximum; if it is 0, stop; otherwise replace it by floor(max/2).
3. Answer is the sum of the heap.

### Why it works
Exchange argument: the saving from halving a fare a is a - floor(a/2) = ceil(a/2), which is non-decreasing in a, and after a halving the same fare offers a smaller next saving. So the multiset of available savings is "decreasing per fare", and picking the X largest available savings greedily (which the heap does) is optimal. Any plan that gives a coupon to a smaller fare while a larger one exists can be improved by swapping that coupon.

### Complexity
O((N + X) log N) time (each pop/push is log N, and X ≤ 10⁵), O(N) space.

### Python solution
```python
import heapq


def min_total_fare(n, x, cost):
    heap = [-c for c in cost]          # max-heap via negation
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    for _ in range(x):
        top = -heap[0]
        if top == 0:                    # nothing left to reduce
            break
        heapq.heapreplace(heap, -(top // 2))
    return -sum(heap)
```

### Dry run
Fares [1,2,4,128], X=2: heap top 128 -> 64, then top 64 -> 32. Fares are now [1,2,4,32]; the sum is 39.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Stop early once the maximum is 0 (fares of 1 become 0 after one coupon; further coupons do nothing).
- Use 64-bit sums: N·A can reach 10¹⁴.
- X can exceed the useful number of halvings (each fare halves to 0 in about 30 steps); the early exit handles it.
- Floor division, not true halving: 5 becomes 2.

questions.title: Recover distance and time from four mixed-up derived values
questions.statement:
Uber stores derived values instead of distance and time: uSpeed = floor(Distance / Time), uAlpha = Time + Distance, uBeta = Time × Distance and uDelta = Time − Distance. The four values got shuffled and it is not known which is which. For each test case, return the Distance followed by the Time. Assume the absolute value of the distance is always greater than the time. If no such integers exist, return -1, -1.

For example, Time = 10 and Distance = 12 gives uSpeed = 1, uAlpha = 22, uBeta = 120, uDelta = -2, so an input record can be [-2, 1, 22, 120].
questions.explanation: Try the 24 assignments of the four numbers to (speed, alpha, beta, delta). Alpha and delta give d = (alpha - delta)/2 and t = (alpha + delta)/2; they must be integers (equal parity), t is non-zero and |d| > |t|. Accept the assignment if d·t equals beta and floor(d/t) equals speed. O(24) per test.
questions.input_format: T test cases, each with four integers A, B, C, D (the mixed-up values).
questions.output_format: For each test case: Distance then Time, or -1 -1 if impossible.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ T ≤ 100000; -10⁹ ≤ A, B, C, D ≤ 10⁹; time limit 0.5 s.

examples.explanation: Time = 10, Distance = 12 as described above.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
Alpha = d + t and delta = t - d are two linear equations in d and t. Once we know which input is alpha and which is delta, d and t follow immediately, and the other two numbers are only used to check consistency.

### Approach
1. Enumerate every permutation of the four values as (speed, alpha, beta, delta).
2. Compute d = (alpha - delta)/2 and t = (alpha + delta)/2; skip if either division is not exact.
3. Skip if t = 0 or |d| <= |t| (the problem guarantees |d| > |t|).
4. Check d·t = beta and floor(d/t) = speed. The first assignment passing all checks is the answer; otherwise answer [-1, -1].

### Why it works
Alpha and delta uniquely determine (d, t), and beta and speed are fully determined by (d, t). So a candidate assignment is correct exactly when all four stated relations hold. Trying all 24 permutations covers every possible labelling.

### Complexity
O(24) = O(1) per test case, so O(T) overall; O(1) extra space. Python integers avoid overflow of d·t (up to about 10¹⁸).

### Python solution
```python
from itertools import permutations


def recover(values):
    """values = [A, B, C, D], a mix of speed, alpha (d+t), beta (d*t), delta (t-d).
    Returns [distance, time] or [-1, -1]."""
    for speed, alpha, beta, delta in permutations(values):
        if (alpha - delta) % 2 or (alpha + delta) % 2:
            continue
        d = (alpha - delta) // 2       # alpha - delta = 2d
        t = (alpha + delta) // 2       # alpha + delta = 2t
        if t == 0 or abs(d) <= abs(t):
            continue
        if d * t == beta and d // t == speed:
            return [d, t]
    return [-1, -1]
```

### Dry run
Values [-2, 1, 22, 120]. The permutation speed=1, alpha=22, beta=120, delta=-2 gives d = (22+2)/2 = 12, t = (22-2)/2 = 10; |12| > |10|, 12·10 = 120 and floor(12/10) = 1, so the answer is [12, 10].

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Check parity before dividing: alpha - delta must be even.
- Guard t = 0 before computing floor(d/t).
- Use floor (not truncation) if negative values can occur; Python // does this.
- In C++ use 64-bit for d·t.

questions.title: Minimum OTPs to try when equivalent OTPs share letters
questions.statement: A rider must enter an OTP to start an Uber trip. The exact OTP is unknown, but a list of $n$ non-empty OTP strings of lowercase letters is given. To guarantee starting the trip the rider must enter the correct OTP or any OTP equivalent to it. Two OTPs A and B are equivalent if they share at least one common character, or if there is an OTP C in the list that shares a character with A and a character with B. Find the minimum number of OTPs the rider must try to guarantee starting the ride.
questions.explanation: Equivalence is the transitive closure of "shares a letter", so OTPs fall into connected groups, and one attempt per group is both necessary and sufficient. Union the letters of each OTP in a 26-node DSU and count the distinct roots among the OTPs. O(total length) time.
questions.input_format: n, then n strings.
questions.output_format: An integer: minimum number of OTPs to try.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴; each OTP has lowercase letters only and length at most 50; time limit 0.5 s.

examples.explanation: "a", "b" and "ab" are equivalent; "d" is isolated.
Only one OTP, so it must be tried.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
Build a graph whose vertices are OTPs and whose edges join OTPs sharing a letter. "Equivalent" is then "in the same connected component", and trying one OTP per component is the minimum.

### Approach
1. Create a DSU over the 26 letters.
2. For each OTP, union every letter of the OTP with its first letter.
3. Two OTPs are in the same component exactly when their first letters have the same DSU root.
4. Count the distinct roots of the first letters of all OTPs.

### Why it works
If two OTPs share a letter they share a DSU set. If A-C and C-B share letters, then A, C and B all land in one set through the letters of C. Conversely, one set can only be formed by chains of shared letters. So DSU components of letters correspond one-to-one with components of OTPs, and any one OTP of a component is equivalent to all the others.

### Complexity
O(sum of lengths · α(26)) time, about 5·10⁵ operations; O(26) extra space for the DSU.

### Python solution
```python
def min_otps(n, otps):
    parent = list(range(26))

    def find(a):
        while parent[a] != a:
            parent[a] = parent[parent[a]]
            a = parent[a]
        return a

    for s in otps:
        first = ord(s[0]) - 97
        for ch in s:
            ra, rb = find(first), find(ord(ch) - 97)
            if ra != rb:
                parent[ra] = rb
    # number of distinct letter-components that appear in some OTP
    return len({find(ord(s[0]) - 97) for s in otps})
```

### Dry run
["a","b","ab","d"]: "a" has only a; "b" only b; "ab" unions a and b; "d" alone. Roots of first letters: a and b share a root, d has its own, so 2 components.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Do not count letters that appear in no OTP.
- Duplicate OTPs are allowed and fall in the same component.
- A single OTP gives 1.
- Comparing every pair of strings is O(n²) and unnecessary.

questions.title: Partition drivers into teams to maximise total similarity
questions.statement: Uber is partnered with $N$ drivers numbered $1..N$. For each pair $(i, j)$ their similarity is an integer $S_{i,j}$ with $S_{i,j} = S_{j,i}$ and $S_{i,i} = 0$. Uber divides the drivers into any number of teams; each driver is in exactly one team. For every pair $i < j$ in the same team, Uber reduces its efforts by $S_{i,j}$ points. Find the maximum possible total effort Uber can reduce. A team may be of any size.
questions.explanation: Because N ≤ 16, run a subset DP: gain[mask] is the sum of S over pairs inside mask, dp[mask] is the best partition value of mask. For dp[mask], force the lowest set driver into the team and enumerate the submasks of the rest. Total cost is O(3^N).
questions.function_signature: long long solution(int n, vector<vector<int>> s)
questions.input_format: N, then the N×N symmetric similarity matrix.
questions.output_format: The maximum total reduction (64-bit).
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 16; |S[i][j]| up to about 10⁹ (the exponent is partly cropped); S[i][i] = 0; S[i][j] = S[j][i]; time limit 2 s.

examples.explanation: Teams {1,3} and {2}.
One team {1,2,3,4}: 5 pairs of 10 and one pair of -1.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
This is "set partition" with a pairwise score. A team of size k contributes the sum of all its C(k,2) pair similarities. With N ≤ 16 we can afford to try all subsets of subsets.

### Approach
1. gain[mask] = sum of S[i][j] for all pairs i<j inside mask (built incrementally from the mask without its lowest bit).
2. dp[0] = 0. For dp[mask]: let low be the lowest set bit. Enumerate every submask sub of mask without low; the team is sub | low.
3. dp[mask] = max over these teams of gain[team] + dp[mask ^ team].
4. Answer dp[full].

### Why it works
Every partition has exactly one team containing the lowest driver of the current mask, so forcing it into the chosen team enumerates each partition once and does not miss any. The remaining drivers are an independent subproblem because the score is a sum over pairs within teams only.

### Complexity
O(3^N) for the submask enumeration (about 4.3·10⁷ for N = 16) plus O(2^N · N) for gain; O(2^N) memory. In Python the full 3^16 loop is slow; the same algorithm in C++ meets the 2 s limit.

### Python solution
```python
def max_effort(n, s):
    full = (1 << n) - 1
    # gain[mask] = sum of s[i][j] over pairs i<j inside mask
    gain = [0] * (1 << n)
    for mask in range(1, 1 << n):
        low = (mask & -mask).bit_length() - 1
        rest = mask & (mask - 1)
        g = gain[rest]
        m = rest
        while m:
            j = (m & -m).bit_length() - 1
            g += s[low][j]
            m &= m - 1
        gain[mask] = g
    NEG = float('-inf')
    dp = [NEG] * (1 << n)
    dp[0] = 0
    for mask in range(1, 1 << n):
        low = mask & -mask               # the lowest driver must be in some team
        rest = mask ^ low
        sub = rest
        best = NEG
        while True:
            team = sub | low
            v = gain[team] + dp[mask ^ team]
            if v > best:
                best = v
            if sub == 0:
                break
            sub = (sub - 1) & rest
        dp[mask] = best
    return dp[full]
```

### Dry run
Example 1: gain[{1,3}] = 8, gain[{1,2}] = 5, gain[{2,3}] = -10, gain[{1,2,3}] = 3. dp[{1,2,3}] = max(gain[{1}] + dp[{2,3}] = 0 + 0, gain[{1,2}] + dp[{3}] = 5, gain[{1,3}] + dp[{2}] = 8, gain[{1,2,3}] = 3) = 8.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Negative similarities: splitting teams is sometimes better, so never assume one big team.
- Initialise dp with -infinity and always include the "alone" option via sub = 0.
- Use 64-bit values (a team of 16 can sum 120 values of ±10⁹).
- Enumerate submasks of rest = mask ^ low, not of mask, to avoid counting each partition many times.
questions.notes: The exact magnitude bound of S is cropped in the screenshot; sums use 64-bit integers.

questions.title: Place supplied bricks on the tower day by day (descending order)
questions.statement: You build a tower over $N$ days from bricks of distinct sizes (a permutation of $1..N$), one supplied per day. Rules: (1) larger bricks go at the bottom; (2) smaller bricks go on top; (3) a new brick cannot be put on the tower until all larger bricks have been placed. For each day $i$, return the list of brick sizes that can be put on the tower on that day, in descending order. If no brick can be placed on a day, that line is empty.
questions.explanation: Track next = the largest size not yet placed. After brick arr[i] arrives, keep placing next, next-1, ... while that size has already arrived. Each brick is placed once, so O(N) total.
questions.input_format: N, then N integers: the brick size supplied each day.
questions.output_format: N lists, the i-th being the bricks placed on day i in descending order.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 100000; 1 ≤ size ≤ N; all sizes distinct; time limit 1 s.

examples.explanation: Day 2: 5 has arrived so 5 and 4 can be placed. Days 3-4: 3 has not arrived. Day 5: 3, 2, 1.
Placed on the day it arrives.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
The tower must be built strictly in order N, N-1, ..., 1. A brick can only be used once every larger brick is already on the tower, so we are only waiting for the next needed size to show up.

### Approach
1. Keep need = N and a boolean array arrived[].
2. On day i mark arr[i] as arrived and start an empty list for the day.
3. While need >= 1 and arrived[need]: append need to today and decrement need.
4. Record the list for that day (possibly empty).

### Why it works
The set of placed bricks is always {need+1..N}. A brick can be placed exactly when all larger ones are placed and it has arrived, which is the loop condition. Each day we place the maximal run, so nothing placeable is delayed.

### Complexity
O(N) time since need only decreases and each brick is appended once; O(N) space.

### Python solution
```python
def tower_days(n, arr):
    arrived = [False] * (n + 2)
    need = n                        # the largest brick not yet placed
    out = []
    for size in arr:
        arrived[size] = True
        today = []
        while need >= 1 and arrived[need]:
            today.append(need)
            need -= 1
        out.append(today)
    return out
```

### Dry run
arr = [4,5,1,2,3], need = 5. Day 1: 4 arrives, 5 has not -> []. Day 2: 5 arrives -> place 5, 4 (4 already here), need = 3 -> [5,4]. Days 3-4: 1 and 2 arrive but 3 is missing -> []. Day 5: 3 arrives -> place 3, 2, 1 -> [3,2,1].

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Empty days must still print an empty line.
- The sorted-set approach in the screenshot also works, but the boolean array is simpler and O(N).
- Bricks are a permutation of 1..N, so need never goes below 0 incorrectly.
questions.notes: This is the well-known "building a tower of disks" simulation.

questions.title: Minimum charging speed to charge all EVs within the allotted hours
questions.statement: Uber has a fleet of EVs with different battery needs. Given the array evBatteries, where evBatteries[i] is the kWh needed to fully charge the i-th EV, and the total number of hours totalHours by which all EVs must be fully charged, find the minimum charging speed (kWh per hour) of the port so that all EVs are charged in time. Once an EV starts charging at a port it occupies that port for the entire hour, even if it fills before the hour ends. EVs are charged one after another, so the hours add up.
questions.explanation: At speed s an EV with b kWh needs ceil(b/s) hours, and total hours is non-increasing in s. Binary search the smallest s in [1, max(b)] for which the total is at most totalHours.
questions.input_format: evBatteries array and totalHours.
questions.output_format: The minimum integer speed.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ len(evBatteries) ≤ 10⁵; 1 ≤ evBatteries[i] ≤ 10⁹; 1 ≤ totalHours ≤ 10⁹ (the exponent of the last bound is partly cropped); time limit 0.5 s.

examples.explanation: At 120 kWh/h the EVs need 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 6 hours.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
Faster ports never take longer, so feasibility is monotone in the speed. That is the signature of a binary search on the answer.

### Approach
1. Define hours(s) = sum over EVs of ceil(b/s).
2. Search s in [1, max(b)]: at max(b) every EV needs exactly 1 hour, which is the best possible.
3. If hours(mid) <= totalHours then mid works, so move hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1.
4. Return lo.

### Why it works
hours(s) is non-increasing in s, so the set of feasible speeds is an up-closed interval [s*, max(b)]. Binary search converges to its left end s*, the minimum feasible speed.

### Complexity
O(N log max(b)) time, about 10⁵ · 30 operations; O(1) extra space.

### Python solution
```python
def min_speed(ev_batteries, total_hours):
    lo, hi = 1, max(ev_batteries)

    def hours(speed):
        return sum((b + speed - 1) // speed for b in ev_batteries)

    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if hours(mid) <= total_hours:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo
```

### Dry run
b = [120,180,240,60], total 6. lo=1, hi=240. mid=120: 1+2+2+1 = 6 <= 6 -> hi=120. mid=60: 2+3+4+1 = 10 > 6 -> lo=61. mid=90: 2+2+3+1 = 8 -> lo=91. mid=105: 2+2+3+1 = 8 -> lo=106. mid=113: 2+2+3+1=8 -> lo=114. ... the search ends at 120.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Use ceiling division (b + s - 1) // s.
- hours can reach 10¹⁴, so use 64-bit in C++.
- If totalHours < number of EVs no speed is feasible (the statement implies this does not occur).
- Upper bound max(b), not sum(b).
questions.notes: Assumes totalHours >= number of EVs (each EV needs at least one hour); otherwise no speed works.

questions.title: Longest same-type plant segment with at most k replacements
questions.statement: Sam has $n$ plants of various types in a row, given as a string $s$ of lowercase letters ($1 \le n \le 5 \cdot 10^5$). He wants a long continuous segment of plants of one type, and can replace at most $k$ plants ($0 \le k \le 5 \cdot 10^4$) by new plants of any type (a plant cannot be swapped with another plant in the row). Find the maximum possible length of a continuous segment of plants of the same type after at most $k$ replacements.
questions.explanation: For a fixed target letter, slide a window and count the letters different from it; shrink while the count exceeds k. Do this for each of the 26 letters. O(26 n).
questions.input_format: String s, then integer k.
questions.output_format: The maximum segment length.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 5·10⁵; 0 ≤ k ≤ 5·10⁴; lowercase letters; time limit 0.5 s.

examples.explanation: Replace the b at index 1 by a to get "aaaab", with a run of 4 a.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
The final segment consists of one letter c. Every plant in the window that is not c must be replaced, so a window is valid when (#non-c) <= k.

### Approach
1. Fix a target letter ch among the letters present.
2. Move the right pointer; count plants different from ch in the window.
3. While the count exceeds k, advance the left pointer (decrement the count if the leaving plant differs from ch).
4. Track the maximum window length over all ch.

### Why it works
For a fixed ch the validity "non-ch count <= k" is monotone: shrinking a valid window keeps it valid. So for each right end the left pointer only moves forward, and the largest valid window ending at each right end is found. Maximising over all letters covers every possible target type.

### Complexity
O(26 · n) time, O(1) extra space (O(n) for the input).

### Python solution
```python
def longest_same_segment(s, k):
    best = 0
    for ch in set(s):                       # fix the target type
        left = bad = 0
        for right, c in enumerate(s):
            if c != ch:
                bad += 1
            while bad > k:
                if s[left] != ch:
                    bad -= 1
                left += 1
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
```

### Dry run
s = "abaab", k = 1, ch = a. Right moves: a(0 bad), b(1 bad) window [0,1] size 2, a size 3, a size 4, b makes bad = 2 > 1 so left moves past index 1: window [2,4] size 3. Best is 4.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- k = 0 gives the longest existing run.
- k >= n gives n.
- The 26-pass version is fine; a single pass with a max-frequency counter also works.
- The replaced plant is a brand new plant, so any type is possible; there is no need to borrow a plant from elsewhere.

questions.title: Smallest lexicographical subsequence of size k (ride hubs)
questions.statement: Uber must select new ride hubs for expansion. Each potential hub has an integer identifier, and only $k$ hubs can be selected in this phase. Select the lexicographically smallest subsequence of size $k$ from the array hubs.
questions.explanation: Monotonic stack: pop a larger top while a smaller new element arrives and enough elements remain to still fill k places, then push only if the stack has fewer than k elements. O(n).
questions.input_format: hubs array and k.
questions.output_format: The chosen subsequence of size k.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ hubs.size ≤ 10⁵; 1 ≤ hubs[i] ≤ 10⁹; 1 ≤ k ≤ 10⁵ (k ≤ hubs.size); time limit 2 s.

examples.explanation: This is the lexicographically smallest subsequence of length 4.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
To make the sequence small, we want small values as early as possible. A larger earlier value can be dropped whenever a smaller one comes later and we can still reach k elements.

### Approach
1. Scan left to right with a stack.
2. While the top is larger than the current element and (stack size - 1 + elements left including current) >= k, pop.
3. If the stack has fewer than k elements, push the current element.
4. The stack at the end is the answer.

### Why it works
Invariant: the stack is the lexicographically smallest valid prefix of the answer among choices from the elements seen so far. Popping a larger top for a smaller element improves the earlier position, and the "enough remaining" condition guarantees we can still finish with k elements. Not pushing when full ensures the result is exactly k long.

### Complexity
O(n) time since each element is pushed and popped at most once; O(k) space.

### Python solution
```python
def smallest_subsequence(hubs, k):
    stack = []
    n = len(hubs)
    for i, h in enumerate(hubs):
        # pop larger tops while enough elements remain to still reach size k
        while stack and stack[-1] > h and len(stack) - 1 + (n - i) >= k:
            stack.pop()
        if len(stack) < k:
            stack.append(h)
    return stack
```

### Dry run
hubs = [3,1,5,3,5,9,2], k=4. Push 3. 1 < 3 and enough left -> pop 3, push 1. Push 5, then 3 pops 5 (left count enough) -> [1,3]. 5 -> [1,3,5]. 9 -> [1,3,5,9]. 2 arrives: stack full length 4; 9 > 2 and remaining condition 3 + 1 >= 4 holds -> pop 9, push 2 -> [1,3,5,2].

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Equal elements are not popped (strict >), which keeps the earliest and is still lexicographically minimal.
- Without the remaining-count check the stack could end too short.
- k = n returns the array itself.

questions.title: Shortest path from any taxi stand to a passenger on a city grid
questions.statement: A city grid of size $m \times n$ has roads (0) and buildings (1). Several taxi stands are placed on the grid, each given by (row, column). Write a function that finds the shortest path from any taxi stand to a given passenger location, avoiding buildings. The taxi moves up, down, left or right. Return the list of coordinates of the shortest path from a taxi stand to the passenger; if no path exists, return an empty list.
questions.explanation: Run a multi-source BFS from every taxi stand at once, remembering each cell parent, and stop when the passenger is dequeued. Rebuild the path from parents. O(mn).
questions.function_signature: vector<vector<int>> solution(vector<vector<int>> grid, vector<vector<int>> taxi_stands, vector<int> passenger)
questions.input_format: grid, taxi_stands (list of coordinates), passenger (coordinate).
questions.output_format: List of coordinates of the path, or an empty list.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ cells ≤ 20×20; at least one taxi stand; the passenger is always on a road; time limit 0.5 s.

examples.explanation: The stand at (0,0) reaches the passenger in 4 moves; the stand at (3,3) is cut off by buildings in row 2 except through column 0, which is much longer.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
Instead of running a BFS from each stand, start one BFS from all stands simultaneously. The first time the BFS reaches the passenger, it has found the shortest path from the nearest stand.

### Approach
1. Put every stand (on a road cell) in the queue with parent None.
2. Pop a cell; if it is the passenger, walk the parent links back to a stand and reverse the list.
3. Otherwise push each unvisited road neighbour in the four directions, recording its parent.
4. If the queue empties, return []

### Why it works
BFS explores cells in non-decreasing distance from the set of sources, so the first time the passenger is dequeued its distance to the nearest stand is minimal, and the parent chain is a shortest path.

### Complexity
O(m·n) time and space; for 20×20 that is at most 400 cells.

### Python solution
```python
from collections import deque


def shortest_taxi_path(grid, taxi_stands, passenger):
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    prev = {}
    dq = deque()
    for r, c in taxi_stands:                     # multi-source BFS
        if grid[r][c] == 0 and (r, c) not in prev:
            prev[(r, c)] = None
            dq.append((r, c))
    target = tuple(passenger)
    while dq:
        r, c = dq.popleft()
        if (r, c) == target:
            path = []
            cur = target
            while cur is not None:
                path.append(list(cur))
                cur = prev[cur]
            return path[::-1]
        for dr, dc in ((-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)):
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < m and 0 <= nc < n and grid[nr][nc] == 0 and (nr, nc) not in prev:
                prev[(nr, nc)] = (r, c)
                dq.append((nr, nc))
    return []
```

### Dry run
Queue starts with (0,0) and (3,3). (0,0) expands to (1,0); (1,0) to (2,0), (1,1); (1,1) to (1,2); (1,2) to (1,3) = passenger. Parent chain: (1,3) <- (1,2) <- (1,1) <- (1,0) <- (0,0).

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- A taxi stand on a building cell cannot be used.
- Passenger already on a stand gives a one-cell path.
- Neighbour order decides which shortest path is returned when ties exist.
- Mark cells visited when they are enqueued, not when popped.

questions.title: Binary prefixes divisible by 5 (fleet codes)
questions.statement: Each Uber car is represented by a binary array `codes`, 0-indexed. Let $x_i$ be the number whose binary representation is the subarray codes[0..i] (most significant bit first). For example, if codes = [1, 0, 1], then $x_0 = 1$, $x_1 = 2$, $x_2 = 5$. Return an array of booleans where the $i$-th entry is true if $x_i$ is divisible by 5.
questions.explanation: Keep only the remainder mod 5: rem = (2·rem + bit) mod 5, and output rem == 0. O(n) with no big numbers.
questions.input_format: Binary array codes.
questions.output_format: Boolean array.

examples.explanation: The prefixes are 1, 2, 5 in decimal; only the last is divisible by 5.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
Each prefix equals the previous prefix doubled plus the new bit. Divisibility by 5 only depends on the remainder, so we never need the (huge) number itself.

### Approach
1. rem = 0.
2. For each bit: rem = (rem·2 + bit) mod 5.
3. Append (rem == 0).

### Why it works
x_i = 2·x_{i-1} + bit_i, and (2a + b) mod 5 = (2·(a mod 5) + b) mod 5, so the remainder recurrence is exact.

### Complexity
O(n) time, O(1) extra space (O(n) output).

### Python solution
```python
def prefixes_div_by_5(codes):
    out = []
    rem = 0
    for bit in codes:
        rem = (rem * 2 + bit) % 5      # keep only the remainder
        out.append(rem == 0)
    return out
```

### Dry run
codes = [1,0,1]: rem = 1 -> false; rem = (2+0) = 2 -> false; rem = (4+1) mod 5 = 0 -> true.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Do not build the integer: with 10⁵ bits it overflows 64-bit.
- Output booleans in the exact language format required (true/false).
- A leading 0 bit keeps rem = 0, so x = 0 counts as divisible by 5.

questions.title: Count notification orders consistent with a visible-count log
questions.statement:
A driver receives trip notifications, each shown with size proportional to the trip amount (all amounts are distinct). A new notification covers every earlier visible notification of smaller amount; a notification with a smaller amount than the last visible one does not cover it. For example, amounts 20, 10, 40, 30 give visible counts A = 1, 2, 1, 2. The logging system recorded the sequence A_1..A_N, where A_i is the number of visible notifications after i notifications have arrived. Count the permutations of trip amounts (arrival orders) that could produce the log, modulo $10^9+7$. If the log is inconsistent, the answer is 0.

Input: each test case has N and then A_1..A_N. Constraints: $1 \le A_i \le i$; $2 \le N \le 10^5$.
questions.explanation: A_i is the size of a monotonic (decreasing) stack. The log fixes the previous-greater index of every position. The permutation must make each position the maximum of its segment (previous greater, end of its subtree], and these segments are nested, so the count is N! / product of segment lengths (mod p).
questions.input_format: Per test case: N, then N integers A_1..A_N.
questions.output_format: One line per test case: the number of permutations modulo 1000000007.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ A_i ≤ i; 2 ≤ N ≤ 10⁵; the amounts are distinct but the log values may repeat.

examples.explanation: Four orderings of 5 amounts produce visible counts 1,2,3,1,2.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
The visible notifications form a stack where an arriving amount removes every smaller amount on top. So A_i = A_{i-1} + 1 - (number popped). Equivalently A_i is the length of the chain "previous greater of previous greater ..." ending at i. The log therefore determines, for each position i, its previous-greater index pg(i) (the last j < i with A_j = A_i - 1).

### Approach
1. Validate: A_1 = 1 and A_i <= A_{i-1} + 1, A_i >= 1; otherwise answer 0.
2. Compute pg(i) = last index seen at level A_i - 1 (0 if A_i = 1).
3. Compute end(i) = (next index with A <= A_i) - 1, the last position of the subtree of i.
4. The requirement "pg(i) is the previous greater" is equivalent to: pi_i is the maximum of positions pg(i)+1 .. end(i). The size of that segment is end(i) - pg(i).
5. Answer = N! / prod(end(i) - pg(i)) modulo p, using a modular inverse.

### Why it works
The segments (pg(i), end(i)] are nested or disjoint (a laminar family), and in each one the owner i must hold the maximum. For a random permutation the events "owner i is the maximum of its segment" are independent over a laminar family where each segment has its own owner, giving probability prod 1/len. Multiplying by N! counts the permutations. Brute force over all permutations for N up to 7 confirms the formula for every achievable log.

### Complexity
O(N) time using stacks, plus one modular exponentiation; O(N) space.

### Python solution
```python
MOD = 10**9 + 7


def count_permutations(n, a):
    """a[i] = number of visible notifications after i+1 arrivals."""
    if a[0] != 1:
        return 0
    last = {0: 0}                      # last[level] = 1-based index of the latest element at that stack size
    pg = [0] * (n + 2)                 # previous-greater index (0 = none)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        h = a[i - 1]
        if h < 1 or h - 1 not in last:
            return 0
        pg[i] = last[h - 1]
        last[h] = i
        for key in [k for k in last if k > h]:     # deeper levels are closed
            del last[key]
    # end[i] = last position of i's subtree = (next index with level <= level_i) - 1
    end = [n] * (n + 2)
    stack = []
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        while stack and a[stack[-1] - 1] >= a[i - 1]:
            end[stack.pop()] = i - 1
        stack.append(i)
    fact = 1
    for v in range(2, n + 1):
        fact = fact * v % MOD
    denom = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        denom = denom * (end[i] - pg[i]) % MOD
    return fact * pow(denom, MOD - 2, MOD) % MOD
```

### Dry run
A = [1,2,3,1,2]: pg = [0,1,2,0,4]; end = [3,3,3,5,5]; lengths = [3,2,1,5,1], product 30, 5!/30 = 120/30 = 4.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Reject logs with A_1 != 1 or jumps larger than +1.
- Segment lengths are at most N < p so they are invertible modulo 10⁹+7.
- Use a dictionary or array indexed by level to find the latest index per level; delete deeper levels as they close.
- Amounts are distinct, so there are no ties between amounts; only the log can repeat.
questions.notes: The full set of samples is not visible; the rule "a new notification covers earlier visible ones with a smaller amount" is inferred from the 20/10/40/30 narration and checked by brute force over all permutations for N up to 7.

questions.title: Maximum visitable countries on a tree with paired COVID permissions
questions.statement:
Uber starts a flight service between $n$ countries connected by $n-1$ bidirectional routes forming a tree. Each country is either Open (O) or Restricted (R). Flights can visit only Open countries (a flight cannot land in or take off from a Restricted one). Uber can obtain special permissions to turn some Restricted countries to Open, but permissions are issued only in pairs (two at a time), and requesting more permissions than the number of Restricted countries is illegal (ERROR 404). For each country, determine the maximum number of countries that can be visited by flights originating there, assuming optimal conversion of Restricted countries; the permissions for different starting countries are independent. If the home country is Restricted and does not get permission, no flight can take off from it. Return the sum of these values (fits in 64-bit).

Input: $n$ ($1 \le n \le 50005$); a string of length $n$ over O and R; an array of $n-1$ integers where the $i$-th element (1-indexed) is the country connected to country $i+1$.
questions.explanation: For each start, we want the largest connected piece of the tree containing it that uses at most K Restricted nodes, where K is the largest even number not above the count of R. This is a tree knapsack (dp over (node, conversions used)). The fast intended solution is not recovered; the provided DP is correct but cubic-ish overall.
questions.function_signature: long long solution(int n, string s, vector<int> a)
questions.input_format: n, then the status string, then the n-1 route endpoints.
questions.output_format: A single 64-bit integer: the sum over all countries of the maximum visitable countries.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 50005; the routes form a tree; sum fits in 64-bit.

examples.explanation: Per-country answers are [4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5].

questions.solution:
### Intuition
Because only Open countries can be visited, the set of reachable countries from a start v is the connected piece of the tree containing v after the converted countries become Open. Conversions are paired and at most |R|, so effectively we may convert up to K = |R| (rounded down to an even number) Restricted countries; leftover conversions can be wasted on countries that are not in the piece. So for each v we want the largest connected piece containing v with at most K Restricted nodes.

### Approach
1. K = |R| - (|R| mod 2).
2. For a start v, root the tree at v. Let f[u][j] be the maximum size of a connected piece containing u inside the subtree of u that uses exactly j R-nodes (u itself counts if it is R).
3. Merge each child w into u as a knapsack: either skip w, or take a piece f[w][t] and add t to j.
4. The answer for v is max over j <= K of f[v][j] (if v is R and K = 0 the piece is empty, giving 0 since no flight can take off).
5. Sum over all v.

### Why it works
A piece containing v is exactly a subtree-closed choice of a connected set; counting the R nodes in it is a knapsack cost. The DP enumerates all such sets by merging independent child subtrees, so the maximum over j <= K is the best feasible piece. Brute force over all even-sized conversion sets matches the DP on 300 random small trees.

### Complexity
Per start O(n·K) with the usual small-to-large bound on knapsack sizes, so O(n²·K) overall in the worst case; this passes only small inputs. A rerooting or centroid-based method would be needed for n = 50005.

### Python solution
```python
import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(1 << 16)
NEG = -10**9


def flight_sum(n, s, a):
    """s[i] in 'OR' (country i+1); a[i] (1-based) connects country i+2 with country a[i]."""
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for i, p in enumerate(a):
        adj[i + 1].append(p - 1)
        adj[p - 1].append(i + 1)
    r_total = s.count('R')
    k = r_total - (r_total % 2)           # permissions come in pairs and cannot exceed |R|

    def best_from(root):
        # f[v][j] = max countries in a connected piece containing v, inside v's subtree, using j conversions
        order, parent = [], [-1] * n
        stack = [root]
        seen = [False] * n
        seen[root] = True
        while stack:
            u = stack.pop()
            order.append(u)
            for w in adj[u]:
                if not seen[w]:
                    seen[w] = True
                    parent[w] = u
                    stack.append(w)
        f = [None] * n
        for v in reversed(order):
            cost = 1 if s[v] == 'R' else 0
            cur = [NEG] * (k + 1)
            if cost <= k:
                cur[cost] = 1
            for w in adj[v]:
                if w == parent[v]:
                    continue
                child = f[w]
                new = cur[:]                       # option: do not extend into w
                for j in range(k + 1):
                    if cur[j] < 0:
                        continue
                    for t in range(k + 1 - j):
                        if child[t] >= 0 and cur[j] + child[t] > new[j + t]:
                            new[j + t] = cur[j] + child[t]
                cur = new
            f[v] = cur
        return max(f[root])                        # at most k conversions; unused ones go to unreachable R's

    return sum(max(best_from(v), 0) for v in range(n))
```

### Dry run
Sample: R count = 3 so K = 2. Start 1 (R): must convert itself, then one more R: best piece {1,2,3,4} = 4. Start 5 (R): {5,3,4,6,7} = 5. Sum of [4,4,5,5,5,5,5] = 33.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- If the start is R and K = 0 the answer for that start is 0.
- n = 1 works: a single Open country gives 1, a single Restricted gives 0.
- Edge endpoints are 1-indexed: the i-th array element connects country i+1.
- Extra conversions are harmless only while the total stays <= |R|; with |R| odd the last R cannot be converted.
questions.notes: Interpretation (checked on the sample and by brute force): the number of conversions must be even and at most the count of R, so at most K = |R| rounded down to even are usable; extra pairs can always be spent on unreachable R countries. For |R| = 3 this gives K = 2 and matches [4,4,5,5,5,5,5]. The reference DP is O(n·K) per start, which is too slow for n = 50005; an efficient solution was not recovered from the screenshots.

questions.title: Assign riders and drivers in alternating order with maximum rider strength
questions.statement: Uber has a fair with a game for riders and drivers. $N$ participants stand in a row with indices $0..N-1$; participant $i$ has strength $A_i$. Divide them into riders (R) and drivers (D) such that: (1) no two drivers and no two riders have consecutive indices; (2) riders and drivers are equal in number; (3) the total strength of the riders is as large as possible compared with the drivers; (4) everyone is assigned. Output a string of length $N$ of R and D. If several assignments are correct, output the lexicographically smallest.
questions.explanation: Under the literal reading, condition (1) forces an alternating row, so only "RDRD..." and "DRDR..." exist (and N must be even). Pick the one with larger rider strength; on a tie choose "DRDR..." which is lexicographically smaller.
questions.input_format: N, then N strengths.
questions.output_format: A string of length N over R and D.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
If neither two riders nor two drivers may sit next to each other, then the row must alternate, so there are only two candidate answers (when N is even, which condition 2 also needs).

### Approach
1. If N is odd, equal counts are impossible: return an empty string.
2. Compute even = sum of A at even indices and odd = sum at odd indices.
3. If riders sit on even indices (RDRD...), rider strength is even; otherwise (DRDR...) it is odd.
4. Choose RDRD... if even > odd, else DRDR... (on a tie DRDR... is lexicographically smaller since D < R).

### Why it works
Alternation leaves two assignments. Condition 3 asks for the larger rider total (equivalently, maximise riders minus drivers). Comparing the two sums chooses the better; the tie-break follows the lexicographic rule. Brute force over all strings for N up to 8 confirms this.

### Complexity
O(N) time, O(N) output.

### Python solution
```python
def assign(n, a):
    """Alternating assignment; returns an empty string when n is odd (equal counts impossible)."""
    if n % 2:
        return ''
    even = sum(a[0::2])
    odd = sum(a[1::2])
    # riders on even indices -> "RDRD..."; riders on odd indices -> "DRDR..."
    if even > odd:
        return 'RD' * (n // 2)
    return 'DR' * (n // 2)       # odd >= even; on a tie "DR.." is lexicographically smaller
```

### Dry run
A = [1,2,3,4]: even = 1+3 = 4, odd = 2+4 = 6. Odd is larger, so riders are at odd indices: "DRDR".

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Odd N has no valid assignment.
- On a tie compare strings: "DR..." < "RD...".
- If the intended rule only forbids adjacent drivers, a DP over positions would be required instead; the cropped statement does not allow confirming that.
questions.notes: The constraint section and examples are cropped. Condition 1 is ambiguous: read literally ("no two drivers or riders have consecutive indices") it forces alternation; the original intent might only forbid adjacent drivers. The solution implements the literal reading and returns an empty string for odd N.
